cases.abstract: ConvNeXt tests whether the gains associated with hierarchical vision Transformers require attention or can be recovered through convolutional design and modern training. Starting from ResNet, the study fixes an enhanced training recipe and progressively transfers design choices from Swin into a convolutional backbone. The key block separates spatial and channel mixing: a 7 x 7 depthwise convolution acts before fourfold channel expansion, providing a larger spatial receptive field without applying the kernel at the expanded width. At 384 x 384 resolution, ConvNeXt-B trained on ImageNet-1K reaches 85.1% top-1 accuracy versus 84.5% for Swin-B, with V100 inference throughput of 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second. ImageNet-22K pretraining followed by ImageNet-1K fine-tuning yields 87.8% top-1 accuracy for ConvNeXt-XL at the same resolution. Standard detection and segmentation heads yield competitive COCO and ADE20K results, extending the comparison beyond classification. The evidence establishes modernized convolution as a competitive alternative to Swin in these workloads, rather than identifying attention removal as an isolated cause of improvement.
cases.methods: ConvNeXt applies its 7 x 7 depthwise convolution before channel expansion, so the larger spatial kernel operates at the block's narrower width. This mixes locations independently within each channel; the following 1 x 1 convolutions perform channel mixing, expanding width fourfold and then restoring it. Layer normalization precedes these pointwise layers, and a single GELU separates them within a residual block. The ordering keeps the larger spatial operation away from the expanded representation while preserving the separation of spatial and channel processing found in Transformer blocks. A nonoverlapping 4 x 4 stem and normalized, separate downsampling layers complete the hierarchy. The redesign is evaluated sequentially with a fixed 300-epoch AdamW recipe on ImageNet-1K and roughly controlled FLOPs; small-regime accuracies average three seeds. Thus, each comparison concerns a change conditional on the preceding architecture, rather than an independent component effect.
cases.results: An improved training recipe alone raises ResNet-50 accuracy from 76.1% to 78.8%, establishing why architecture should be assessed against the strengthened baseline. Within that fixed recipe, switching ReLU to GELU leaves top-1 accuracy at 80.6%, but reducing the block to one activation raises it to 81.3%. This contrast favors the tested activation layout over activation substitution alone. Separate downsampling initially causes training to diverge; normalization at the stem, stage transitions, and final pooling restores stable training, yielding 82.0% in the completed roadmap versus Swin-T's 81.3%. These gains remain conditional on preceding redesigns. A downstream comparison extends the finding beyond classification: with ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN under a 3x schedule, ConvNeXt-B obtains 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP on COCO, against 53.0 and 45.8 for Swin-B. The COCO comparison supports transfer of the redesigned backbone, while the roadmap identifies combinations that work and substitutions that do not improve accuracy.
cases.notes: Figure 2 and Section 2.6 support the activation and stabilization comparisons; Table 3 supports the COCO transfer comparison. The roadmap's final small-model result is 82.0%, whereas Table 1 reports 82.1% for ConvNeXt-T; these records are not combined. The fixed-recipe roadmap is sequential, not factorial. ImageNet-1K-only training and ImageNet-22K pretraining remain distinct. EfficientNetV2-L leads the listed ImageNet-1K-only accuracy comparisons, so the abstract retains Swin-specific scope. Throughput is measured on a V100, not inferred from FLOPs. Seed averages do not establish statistical significance.

cases.abstract: Interactive exploration of captured scenes requires both fast rendering and sufficient reconstruction quality, a combination not provided by training speed alone. The method represents a static scene with anisotropic 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points, avoiding normal estimation while allowing geometry, opacity, and directional appearance to be optimized. Cloning and splitting refine the primitive allocation, while a tile-based renderer shares a depth ordering across pixels instead of sorting each pixel separately and reconstructs opacity information during backpropagation. This combination supports fast splatting without imposing a fixed limit on the number of blended primitives that receive gradients. Across held-out views from three real-scene datasets, the 30,000-iteration configuration renders at dataset-average rates of 134-154 frames per second on an A6000 after approximately 27-42 minutes of training. Relative to Mip-NeRF360, it has higher SSIM and lower LPIPS on all three datasets, but lower PSNR on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. The speed-quality tradeoff requires hundreds of megabytes of stored parameters, with residual artifacts in weakly observed regions and occasional popping associated with approximate visibility handling.
cases.methods: Efficient splatting requires visibility ordering, but sorting and storing a separate contribution history for every pixel would be costly. The renderer projects each Gaussian to an image-space footprint and duplicates it across overlapping 16 x 16 tiles. Keys combining tile identity and view-space depth permit one GPU radix sort to organize all tile lists. Pixels blend these lists front to back until opacity saturates; sharing the order avoids per-pixel sorting, at the cost of approximate visibility. The backward pass reuses the lists in reverse and reconstructs intermediate opacity factors from saved final accumulations instead of retaining variable-length histories. This keeps the extra per-pixel storage constant while allowing gradients for every blended primitive, without a fixed count cutoff. Optimization updates geometry, opacity, and spherical-harmonic appearance using L1 plus D-SSIM loss, with positional-gradient thresholds triggering cloning of small Gaussians or splitting of large ones.
cases.results: Longer optimization improves reconstruction but changes the deployment cost. On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, moving from 7,000 to 30,000 iterations raises PSNR from 25.60 to 27.21 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.279 to 0.214; rendering drops from 160 to 134 frames per second and stored parameters increase from 523 to 734 MB. The longer-trained model has higher SSIM and lower LPIPS than Mip-NeRF360 on this dataset, yet falls below its 27.69 dB PSNR, so the quality comparison remains metric-dependent. A separate ablation exposes the cost of restricting gradients. With manually downsampled inputs for Truck, Garden, and Bicycle, updating only the ten frontmost Gaussians yields 19.19 dB average PSNR after 30,000 iterations, versus 26.05 dB for the full method, and causes unstable optimization. Preserving gradients is therefore consequential in these scenes, although the full method still leaves artifacts under weak coverage and occasional visibility-related popping.
cases.notes: Main metrics use every eighth image as a test view. Mip-NeRF360's own-dataset quality metrics are imported; other comparisons use reruns. Its reported 48 hours is 48 A100 GPU-hours from a four-GPU, 12-hour run, not an A6000 wall-time measurement. Table 1 supports the optimization tradeoff; Table 3 supports the gradient-cutoff finding on three scenes with manually downsampled inputs. Stored-parameter memory excludes training peaks and rasterizer workspace. Random initialization on bounded synthetic scenes does not establish comparable reconstruction in real captures.
